finding.claim: PUT /me mass-assigns the entire request body onto the authenticated user's record and persists it, letting a user set privileged or ownership fields (role, isAdmin, id, tenantId, emailVerified, password hash). Severity HIGH is conditional on the user schema containing such fields; otherwise MEDIUM.
finding.source: req.body in PUT /me handler (attacker-controlled by any authenticated user)
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) at users.js:5, then req.store.save(req.user) at users.js:6

trace.note: Object.assign merges entire req.body into req.user with no allowlist
res.json(req.user) echoes the attacker-set values back

finding.guards_checked: No field allowlist, no schema validation, no key rejection in users.js. Auth enforcement for /me and the req.user/req.store population are not in the repo (route mounting and middleware unverified).

verdict.guard_found: none. users.js:5 is an unfiltered Object.assign(req.user, req.body), and users.js:6 persists it with a bare req.store.save call whose result is unused. No allowlist, schema check, or key rejection appears in the file. The /me auth middleware and req.store implementation are not in the directory, so they could not be checked.
verdict.reason: The trace matches users.js:4-7 exactly, and users.js:5-6 writes every attacker-supplied body key onto req.user and persists it with no filter, so any caller that reaches this route (authenticated, per the candidate's assumption) can alter its own record. Whether that yields privilege escalation depends on the user schema and on whether req.store.save filters fields, neither of which is in the repo, so the HIGH severity stays conditional while the mass-assignment flaw itself is confirmed.

finding.claim: A JSON body with a '__proto__' key invokes the __proto__ setter on req.user via Object.assign's [[Set]] semantics, replacing req.user's prototype with an attacker-chosen object. Impact is scoped to req.user (no global Object.prototype pollution) and depends on downstream inherited-property reads such as req.user.isAdmin. Medium severity; not independent of BIZ-1.
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) at users.js:5 triggering the Object.prototype.__proto__ setter on req.user

trace.note: Object.assign copies own enumerable '__proto__' key from parsed JSON body using [[Set]]
req.user (with altered prototype) is passed to store.save; serialization behavior unverified

finding.guards_checked: No __proto__/constructor/prototype key rejection and no null-prototype record in users.js. Downstream authorization code that reads inherited properties is not in the repo.

verdict.guard_found: none. users.js has no __proto__/constructor/prototype key filtering and no null-prototype record (users.js:4-6). The repo contains no auth middleware, store implementation, or downstream authorization code, so nothing else in the repo can be checked.
verdict.reason: The mechanism is real: a JSON-parsed body yields an own "__proto__" key, and Object.assign at users.js:5 uses [[Set]], so it invokes the Object.prototype.__proto__ setter on req.user. Whether that is a security issue cannot be decided from the repo: the attacker is whoever can reach PUT /me (an authenticated user, since req.user must already exist), the prototype change only affects that user's in-request object, and whether it persists depends on store.save (users.js:6) and on downstream code reading inherited properties such as isAdmin, neither of which is in the repo.

finding.claim: PUT /me/profile sets displayName and bio unconditionally via Object.assign, so omitted fields become undefined and erase the stored values. Self-affecting logic error; LOW.
finding.source: req.body destructuring of displayName and bio in PUT /me/profile
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, { displayName, bio }) at users.js:12, then req.store.save at users.js:13

trace.note: destructure displayName and bio from req.body; missing keys yield undefined
Object.assign overwrites stored fields with undefined

finding.guards_checked: None in users.js; no presence check before assignment.

verdict.guard_found: none. users.js:11-13 has no presence check, default, or allowlist between req.body and the save. The only other guard in the file is the router mount, which is not shown and does not validate body fields.
verdict.reason: At users.js:11-12, a body missing displayName or bio yields undefined, and Object.assign copies own properties with undefined values, so the stored fields are overwritten and users.js:13 persists them; the attacker is any authenticated user acting only on their own record (req.user), so this is a functional data-loss bug with no privilege impact, consistent with the candidate's LOW rating. Caveat: whether the erasure survives persistence depends on req.store.save, which is not in this directory.

finding.claim: displayName and bio are accepted without type or length validation and stored/returned unchecked, allowing objects, arrays, or very large strings. LOW; injection impact unverified because rendering code is not in the repo.
finding.sink: Persisted via req.store.save at users.js:13 and returned via res.json at users.js:14

trace.note: values extracted from req.body with no type check
values assigned to req.user without validation
stored without length or type limits

finding.guards_checked: No typeof or length checks in users.js. Template or rendering behavior for these fields is not in the repo.

verdict.guard_found: none. users.js:11 destructures displayName and bio from req.body with no typeof or length check. users.js:12 passes them unchecked to Object.assign on req.user. users.js:13 calls req.store.save with no validation, and users.js:14 returns the full req.user. No validation middleware is registered in users.js, and the repo contains no other guard for this route.
verdict.reason: The trace matches users.js:11-14 exactly and no control intercepts the values, so unvalidated displayName/bio are stored and echoed back (users.js:11-14). The attacker is an authenticated user editing their own profile (req.user is set outside this repo), so the practical impact is LOW and mostly self-affecting; any injection or DoS consequence depends on the store driver (not in repo) and on rendering code (not in repo), which I could not verify.

finding.claim: req.store.save is not awaited and the response is sent first, so a save failure (if save is async) becomes an unhandled promise rejection; on Node 15+ this can crash the process, and the client may see success for an unpersisted write. LOW, plausible; depends on the store implementation.
finding.source: Authenticated user input that the store rejects (PUT /me at line 6, PUT /me/profile at line 13)
finding.sink: Unawaited req.store.save(...) at users.js:6 and users.js:13

trace.note: req.store.save called without await or error handling
res.json sent before persistence is confirmed

finding.guards_checked: No await, no .catch, no try/catch in users.js. Whether store.save returns a promise is not in the repo.

verdict.guard_found: none. users.js:6 and users.js:13 are bare `req.store.save(...)` statements with no await, .catch, or try/catch, and the response is sent on the next line (users.js:7, users.js:14). The repo contains no store implementation (the Glob shows only users.js plus .claude/skills files), so whether save returns a promise that can reject is not checkable here.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (users.js:6-7 and users.js:13-14 are unawaited saves followed by res.json), and no guard exists in the repo, but the entire claim depends on whether req.store.save is async and can reject, which the repo does not show; the attacker is only an authenticated user writing their own record (users.js:5, 12), so any impact is reliability/data-integrity rather than an authz flaw.
